research_setting.statement_markdown: The study concerns inference for a scientific parameter $\theta_0$ from observations $W_i$ when auxiliary functions $\eta_0$, such as conditional means, must also be learned from data. landscape.summary_markdown: Orthogonal-score methods and cross-fitting address different parts of estimation with learned nuisance functions. The former makes a target-defining moment $m(\theta,\eta)=\mathbb E[\psi(W;\theta,\eta)]$ locally insensitive to nuisance perturbations, while the latter evaluates scores on observations excluded from the corresponding nuisance fit [Chernozhukov et al., 2018](#cite:citation.orthogonal_scores.2018). Together they offer a way to study inference when nuisance functions are learned flexibly, but neither identifies the target by itself or supplies an unconditional guarantee. This fixture leaves the sampling structure, regularity and required nuisance accuracy unverified.

frameworks.title: Orthogonal population moments
frameworks.formulation_markdown: Let $\theta_0$ satisfy $\mathbb E[\psi(W;\theta_0,\eta_0)]=0$. Neyman orthogonality requires $\left.\partial_t\mathbb E[\psi(W;\theta_0,\eta_0+t h)]\right|_{t=0}=0$ for admissible nuisance directions $h$.
frameworks.assumptions_markdown: The target $\theta_0$ is identified by the population moment. The derivative exists for the declared admissible nuisance directions $h$; integrability and regularity must be stated for any inference claim.
frameworks.explanation_markdown: An orthogonal-score approach represents the target through a population moment and chooses the score so small nuisance errors have no first-order effect on that moment at the truth. Writing $m(\theta,\eta)=\mathbb E[\psi(W;\theta,\eta)]$ with $m(\theta_0,\eta_0)=0$, this requires $$\left.\frac{d}{dt}m(\theta_0,\eta_0+t h)\right|_{t=0}=0$$ for admissible nuisance directions $h$. The construction is useful when $\eta_0$ must be learned before estimating $\theta_0$, because it reduces local sensitivity to that learning error. Identification, differentiability and control of the remaining error are still needed; the condition does not imply global invariance or an inference guarantee on its own.
frameworks.relevance_markdown: Separates the target-defining condition from the construction and estimation of nuisance functions.
limitations: Structural illustration using the existing source fixture, not a new scientific finding.

algorithm_families.title: Cross-fitted estimating equations
algorithm_families.formulation_markdown: Let $I_1,\ldots,I_K$ partition $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and let $\widehat\eta_{-k}$ be fit without fold $I_k$. A pooled estimating equation is $$\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in I_k}\psi(W_i;\widehat\theta,\widehat\eta_{-k})=0.$$ The score and a rule for choosing a solution must be specified.
algorithm_families.assumptions_markdown: The sample structure must permit the declared split, the nuisance fits and moments must be well defined, and sufficient nuisance rates and identification are needed for any asymptotic claim.
algorithm_families.explanation_markdown: Cross-fitting separates nuisance learning from score evaluation by partitioning observations into folds $I_k$ and fitting $\widehat\eta_{-k}$ without fold $k$. The target estimate can then solve $$\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in I_k}\psi(W_i;\widehat\theta,\widehat\eta_{-k})=0.$$ Each observation is evaluated using a nuisance fit that did not train on it, reducing the reuse of fitting errors in the estimating equation. This is an estimation construction for the declared target, not a new target definition; the sampling structure must support the split, and identification, a solution rule and sufficient nuisance accuracy remain necessary for inference.
algorithm_families.computational_requirements_markdown: Fit nuisance functions on $K$ training complements and solve the pooled moment system. Cost depends on the nuisance learner, score evaluation and root solver.

attention_items.context_markdown: For this structural example, the proposed target solves $\mathbb E_{P_0}[\psi(W;\theta_0,\eta_0)]=0$, where $W$ is the observed record, $P_0$ is the enrolled-cohort distribution, $\psi$ defines the target $\theta_0$ and $\eta_0$ is its nuisance function. Intended deployment to a different population with distribution $P_*$ changes which population expectation the conclusion must address. The project instructions do not yet specify substantive observations or that intended use; neither population is established as the actual deployment setting. Choosing the wider population does not establish that it is identified from the available data.
